speechtext:
1 am assured by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Martin) that it is quite clear. The bill says they are required "for public works and general purposes." That is a pretty broad statement. I wonder about these public works and I think we ought to be a little more specific than that. I should like to figure out a way of needling either the parliamentary secretary or preferably the Minister of Finance into giving us some explanation of what the public works are. I think the best thing the minister could do is to bring down a budget and tell us what he wants to spend the money on.
There are times, however, when I wonder how a budget is worked out. I got a glimpse of it the other day when listening to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras). He was boasting about how well they managed the economy and how much they had been saving, but he was not very convincing. At page 187 of Hansard for October 17, he is reported as saying:
October 24, 1978

I often hear that our expenditures have gone from $16 billion to $50 billion- 'Isn't that shocking'? and 'Indeed that is startling.' But nobody adds to that that next year the gross national product of this country will be $250 billion. It has to have a form of relativity-
Why did he bring that notion forward? Is it because the government's expenditures are decided upon by either estimate of what the gross national product is going to be? I wish I could do that in my own domestic financing. I have to know what my revenue is going to be and I have to budget with a margin of safety within my domestic arrangements in order to do it properly.
There are only two things that 1 think any good housekeeper does in the matter of overspending and casting beyond his revenues. One is buying a house and the other may be buying a car, particularly with the price of cars these days. Ele realizes he can use so much of his current revenue for a mortgage or to make a loan-although mortgage rates are pretty frightening these days. But that is not the way the government does things. It estimates in advance what the gross national product will be and says, "We are going to take x per cent as our chunk of the gross national product, because that is the revenue-producing part and we are going to levy taxes against that." Sometimes they make mistakes. What any good manager should know is what the revenue is going to be and keep within that.
I wonder why the government does not deal more with what its revenues are this year and what its forecast of revenues is next year, not in terms of the gross national product but in terms of an addition because of greater employment or expanded business activity, and then work out on a percentage basis if it has to increase its expenditures. Now it is finding it has to pull back. I have to convince myself and my wife that we can afford carrying charges, whether it be for a house or for a car. I cannot understand why the government cannot work that way.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my remarks before the dinner hour I mentioned the many reasons why I am disquieted by this bill, worried and deeply concerned. 1 had reached my fourth reason, that is the contribution the proposed borrowing will make to our national debt. Now I want to look at the growth in that debt.
Let us look at the record of this government in debt accumulation. I put that forward as something that we ought to examine closely when we are being asked to add to that debt by several billion dollars. I repeat what I said earlier several
Borrowing Authority Act
times, that what we are doing is adding to a debt which is going to be assumed by those who follow us, by those serving in this chamber today and who may very well be sitting here ten years from now. Those are the people for whom we should be concerned.
Let us look at the record of the government, which says today that on the road to Bonn the Prime Minister saw the light of restraint. We can think of another road, the one to Damascus. However, a different light fell then. This time the Prime Minister talks about the light of restraint. Can we believe him, Mr. Speaker? You may; I cannot. I will come to the matter of expenditures in due course. What concerns me at the moment is debt and the actual, eventual debt charges.
I have extracted from a reputable publication put out by the Canadian Tax Foundation called "The National Finances" some very interesting statistics about the debt of Canada over the last several years. These statistics are from the latest edition. I have chosen selective years over the past 30 odd to give us a perspective of the growth of the debt in this country. The first date is 1946, just after the war, when the total growth debt was only $18.9 billion. Some 20 years later in 1968 the debt had grown to $32.9 billion. By 1977, the last year for which we have figures, the debt has grown to $80.5 billion. That is $80.5 billion compared to $32.9 billion ten years earlier. Over ten years, the ten years of this government, this is an increase in excess of 150 per cent. That is gross debt.
Let us now look at net debt. There is a distinction which is drawn very carefully here. Time unfortunately does not permit me to delve into it, but I advise those who are interested to have a look at this particular publication. The net debt is when all the earnings have been taken away. In 1946 it was $13 billion. In 1968 it was $16.7 billion, a modest increase in 20 years. I repeat, in 1968 the figure was $16.7 billion. In 1977 the figure was $29.5 billion. As hon. members can see, that figure has almost doubled in ten years. In 20 years there was an increase of $3 billion, while in ten years there was an increase of $ 13 billion. That is what bills like this have done to our debt.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, there has been a war going on, a war on your pocket and my pocket.
Who were the ministers of finance in those years? I remember a certain gentleman who is now the commissioner for the northern pipeline, Mr. Sharp. I remember Mr. Turner. Now we have another minister. I am waiting with bated breath to learn what the debt per capita is likely to be in 1978.
What is the cost of this debt per capita? This is of importance because debt carries interest. In 1946 it amounted to $367 for every man, woman and child in Canada. In 1968 it was $688. In 1977, almost ten years later, it had risen to $2,228, having almost quadrupled in ten years.

In 1946, according to this valuable study by the Canadian Tax Foundation, total expenditures were of the order of $2,800 million. By 1968 they had risen to $12 billion, by 1976 to $38 billion and by 1977 to $42 billion. The 1978 figure is around $50 billion. So in those ten years expenditures had risen from $12 billion to almost $50 billion. Is it any wonder I am worried and that the Canadian people are worried?
Before hon. members opposite point out that the gross national product has also increased, let me turn to the argument that so large a part of government expenditure is dictated by statutes and cannot be reduced. What was said by the President of the Treasury Board when he spoke on this subject during debate on the address? He got in his speech before the government House leader interrupted the debate to bring down this bill about borrowing. On October 17, as reported in Hansard at page 188, the hon. gentleman stated:
On April 1 of this year, the April problem I call it, my people did a tally for me about the inexorable and inevitable growth of spending for next year. As I said publicly, my hair went white. It was far too high. It would have broken through the commitment to stay within the GNP trend line.

We are back with this GNP again. To continue:
Something significant had to be done . . . We took $500 million off this year to cut our ceiling to $48,300 million. We have taken $2 billion off for next year to get from $54,600 million to $52,600 million.
I see I was modest in my estimate when earlier I mentioned $50 billion. The amount is more than $52 billion. That is the sum which is to be spent next year and this, I suppose, has something to do with the extra $10 billion which is to be borrowed. I still do not understand why the government insists that the amount of expenditure has to be tied to the g.n.p. and not to revenue.

I do not see that. If the revenue of the government is the GNP, I think we are all in trouble.
The history of the growth of the public service should also be told. It is staggering. I choose as a starting point the year 1964 when there were about 200,000 public servants. By 1968 the figure was 234,000-I suppose the GNP grew during the same period. By 1976 it was 321,000. In ten years the number had risen from 234,000 to 320,000, a growth of about 33 per cent in ten years. We see in the Speech from the Throne that the government is dedicated to the proposition that there should be cuts in the expenditure. Ministers claim to have made them. They say planned expenditures have been cut by $2 billion.
It is easy to plan an expenditure and then to cut back, because the figure they are cutting back to is $52 billion, the figure I mentioned just now. If I were to go back again to the speech of the President of the Treasury Board, I would find that he made a public commitment to reduce the growth of spending to something below the growth of our gross national product. The government has no regard for what it can collect in revenue. In 1976 the minister said that the government met that commitment. I draw the attention of the House to that year. There was growth up until 1976, and I recollect that a minister of finance decided to get out of the government in 1975. It was just after that that the government decided it should cut back on its commitments. The government claims it met its commitment in 1977-78, and it claims it will meet it again in 1979. How growth from $42 billion to $52 billion in one year, 1978-79, is a reduction in the growth of expenditures I find difficult to understand. The absolute figures could be quoted.
With that indication of the extent to which this government has been committed to expanding expenditures and increasing the national debt, I will rest my case and say that it will be impossible for me to support this bill.

During the past six months of compaigning for the by-election which was held last week I was fortunate to get the know the riding of Eglinton well, and it is, with some statistical variations, urban Canada in microcosm. I am aware of the tradition that a member's first speech in this chamber should be non-partisan in nature. I trust that so far I have fulfilled that obligation.
I would like now to refer specifically to the bill before this House. Although I am a new member of less than ten hours' formal standing, I have had some opportunity to become acquainted with this debate. It seems clear to me that the principles expressed at the polls in Eglinton eight days ago are directly contradicted by Bill C-7.
This bill asks basically four things of the House. First, it asks for authority to increase government borrowing by $7 billion during this fiscal year; second, authority to increase government borrowing by an additional $10 billion in the next fiscal year; third, explicit authority to place all or part of that borrowing in foreign markets; and fourth, explicit authority to maintain all previously authorized borrowings in perpetuity, if the government chooses, as a charge against the people of Canada.
On the issue of credibility, on March 16 of this year, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) acknowledged that $21 billion of borrowing authority obtained in three separate instalments was sufficient to meet all cash requirements for the fiscal year 1977-78 and the fiscal year 1978-79, plus a margin for contingencies. Seven months and three days later, the minister informs the House of the need for an additional $7 billion-a 33 per cent increase over the total cash needs he forecast for two years.
The same minister, while steadfastly refusing to discuss his projected budgetary deficit beyond the figure of $10.9 billion, admitted in the spring, some six months ago, and reluctantly confessed, to a $300 million increase in cash needs. Presumably that $300 million is covered by this request, but in addition he suddenly discovered a need for an additional $6.7 billion. He still refuses to give budgetary deficit forecasts when the most conservative figures-and I use that adjective deliberately-indicate a minimum $13 billion deficit which could soar to $15 billion to $16 billion. This government has a credibility problem, and it need look no further than this sort of behaviour for the reason.

In Bill C-7 the government is requesting an additional $7 billion of borrowing power. My generation was taught that it was good to pay one's bills and live within one's means. Certainly the present generation of finance ministers are not the least bit concerned about that. In 1978 borrowings amounting to $38 billion have been authorized. Bill C-45 requested $7 billion, Bill C-ll requested
Borrowing Authority Act
$9 billion, Bill C-31 requested $5 billion, and now Bill C-7 is requesting $17 billion. This total of $38 billion means that each one of us is paying interest on over $7,000. Through the produce of this nation, every citizen will have to pay 10 per cent or in excess of $700. In many instances people in Canada are living on annual income of $3,000, and that $700 is a very large amount of money for them to shoulder.
Those members who were involved in the recent by-elections are aware that the average citizen is now concerned about the amount of money borrowed, and the difficulties faced in an attempt to retain stability in our money. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) was involved in borrowing to sustain the dollar years ago when he was a cabinet minister in the government of the day. That government decided to borrow in order to sustain the Canadian dollar. Canada was faced with extreme financial difficulties because of that measure. It turned out to be totally unsuccessful in the end. In an attempt to maintain the Canadian dollar at 85 cents, an awful lot of money has come out of the pockets of Canadians which has not brought much in return.
I am no financial expert. I have not studied the financial structure to the extent that I know all the answers. In fact, I am not sure whether the new economists will be able to say any more than I. I consider their knowledge to be zero as well. Not long ago I read a newsletter which indicated the United States borrowed so much money a few years ago that it is having a great deal of difficulty making the repayment which is now due. Apparently the money was borrowed in Europe, on terms that it would be repaid in one of two currencies when the term expired, either gold or Swiss francs. Also the newsletter indicated that United States treasury representatives went to Switzerland in an attempt to persuade the Swiss to devalue their money and print more so that there would be enough francs to go around. Rightly so, the Swiss told the Americans there was no deal. There is not enough money in the American treasury at Fort Knox to pay off that loan in gold, particularly with the price of gold today.
Apparently our dollar is worth approximately 84 cents compared to the American currency. One must remember that the Americans are bankrupt. They may not be able to pay the debt incurred in Europe because they will have to pay it in a currency which they do not have. When the deal was made, gold was worth $35 an ounce; today it is worth considerably over $200 an ounce in the United States. They paid large interest payments over the years for that loan, and it will be necessary to pay off the remaining debt at a rate five times what it was incurred at. The United States is not in a very good position, yet we weigh our dollar at 84 cents against the American dollar.
Another government newsletter indicated that three years ago $1 Canadian bought 300 Japanese yen; now it buys 162 Japanese yen. That means our money is worth approximately 50 or 51 cents on the Japanese exchange market. We are in serious difficulty, as is the United States. Even countries which find their currencies rising rapidly are in trouble, because

There is still a valuable commodity out there under the minister's jurisdiction, and that is gold. We are not unaware of this. One of the minister's own colleagues has authorized a publication which indicates that the government has 200,000 gold coins containing half an ounce of pure gold for sale at $150 each. That is a good bargain because gold is going to go up to $300 an ounce, and as the value of the dollar goes down the value of the gold goes up. I suggest the value will go to $300 an ounce by early March. It is now selling on trade markets at from $262 to $267 Canadian funds. We are selling these coins for $150 and the government is going to make some money.
When we have talked about putting out a bullion coin containing one true ounce of .999 fine 22-carat, we have found that we do not have enough gold in this country to produce them. We are somewhat like the United States which found that when it had to pay off its debt in gold it did not have a sufficient amount.
In my part of the country there is still a lot of gold. I suppose there are two or three thousand mines there which operated when gold was selling at $35 an ounce. When I started to work underground in a gold mine I received 58 cents an hour. Things have improved since then. I think my highest

hourly wage was $1.19 as a raiseman, which is a skilled position in a mine.
Let us assume that the same man receives $10 an hour today. It is hard to look back and find that you were making less in a day than a man doing the same job now makes per hour. Gold has increased in price proportionately more. Obviously wages are not going to represent the major portion of the cost of developing gold mining operations. Perhaps the minister should sit down and put together a consortium to pick up some of the gold mining claims throughout northern Ontario, northern Quebec, the maritimes and British Columbia. He knows what the projection is in respect of the tonnage in each one of those holes in the ground. He could get that information from his computers in a matter of a few weeks. When things were tough under a Conservative government-and maybe things are always tough under Conservative governments-most of the Crown corporations or national corporations were established. My point is that just because one is not in favour of government ownership it does not mean the government should not support something that can be of tremendous value. It is my guess that we would be able to put more people back to work for every dollar used in the redevelopment of these gold mines than for every dollar invested in any other industry we might consider.
When we were considering the manufacture and sale of gold bullion coins we were told we would have to double the production of gold in Canada to meet the projected demand of coin distributors in New York, London and other international marketplaces. Canada has a great advantage over large foreign coin manufacturers in the world today, and specifically over the largest, South Africa, which produces the Kruger rand. The United States does not want to buy South African coins or gold from South Africa. Many countries are looking for a

hedge against inflation and one of the best obvious hedges can be found in gold bullion, gold coins or gold in any of its purer forms.
I think it is safe to say that in my area there are 30 or 40 mines which could be put into operation within a matter of 12 months. Gold mining is a very highly labour-intensive industry, one that would not require a great deal of money to put into operation. I remember suggesting not long ago to an individual in a large corporation of the Weston chain that they should expand operations. He asked me if I knew what the profit was from their plant the previous year. We have a long way to go before we can develop the research and development that will establish a viable manufacturing industry in Canada.
We also have a long way to go to establish a country that others will look at and see that it is financially stable and sound. All we are doing is balancing our trade with our raw resources. We can sell off the last of our timber in British Columbia, in northern Ontario or in Quebec; we can give away our raw materials in our mining industries. Nickel is a valuable commodity, not just to establish currency with, but it is a commodity used in almost all manufacturing throughout the world. We do not sell it as a manufactured commodity, however, but as a raw material. This generation is giving away the last of our birthright in order to try to balance our trade and retain our position in the world.
We will grow more trees if we are lucky and we will grow more wheat if we are lucky, but there comes an end to the amount of land available for trees and cereal grains. We do not even pick peaches, pears and grapes in Canada; we buy them from the United States. I was in the Niagara Peninsula in the last fruit season and you could buy Canadian grapes or Canadian pears and peaches there, but in Toronto I found most of them had come from the United States, not from Niagara. We are destroying whatever heritage we have of natural resources.

Mr. Speaker, that is exactly the point I was making. We used all we had in Canada but we did not have enough even for the Canadian market and had to import fruit from the United States. I said that by the time you got to Toronto, which is 50 or 60 miles from the hon. member's area, you found that commodities in the supermarkets were American. We do not have enough fruit. We make wine out of our grapes. We do not sell grapes here; we import them from California.
We can go into any little confectionery store in Toronto, Ottawa, Winnipeg, or Vancouver and on the shelves there will be commodities from 50 countries. You would have to search very hard to find any Canadian commodity. At Moosonee, a tourist trap in my part of the country, you can pick up a souvenir like a totem pole or a little bear supposed to be carved from soapstone. When you turn it over you find it was
October 24, 1978

manufactured in Japan. We are not going to compete in that field, Mr. Speaker.
We are giving away our basic resources in order to try to float our economy. It is one hell of an expense. When we borrow money, that is a hell of an expense too when every man, woman and child, and every old age pensioner in Canada, owes over $7,000 and we pay 10 per cent on that debt. There are very few countries with the resources to make that possible.
We have some resources, Mr. Speaker, so why are we not in the market? I am talking about bringing gold to a stage where it is .999 per cent pure-I am not suggesting we fabricate it, and I am not suggesting we ask people to go into the jewellery business. I am suggesting that we treat gold as a natural resource and start producing it to balance our payments. It would not be hard to raise $7 billion if we started to mine.
In my area there are several mills. One in particular is now operating at some capacity and is making considerable money. It is interesting that the miners with that company receive one cent per dollar every time the price of gold goes up. It does not amount to very much because they started at $50 or $60, which was considered to be the top. But now each of those miners gets well over $125 because of that one cent per dollar every time Canadian gold goes up. That mine is doing very well.
Kerr Addison has been closing for years. It is one of the largest mines in North America. Not long ago a newspaper article indicated that the life of the mine had been extended for another two years. I suggest they could have extended it for ten years if they had been sure of any stability in the price of gold. That company could mill 5,000 tons per day but it is now milling less than 700 tons per day. If the minister put some money into a consortium he could pick up the other 4,000 tons at a number of small mines in the area which we would operate. He could lease them and pay the owners a royalty per ton. If he did this on a large enough scale we could then afford to repair and rebuild for an increased milling capacity.
Then there is the mine known as the Upper Canada. God only knows who owns it, but the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources should be interested in it because he was one of the people who shut it down when he set up the petroleum corporation. He had a couple of partners and one was the main shareholder. When that partner needed money he took the money that was necessary to operate that mine and bought more stock in the petroleum company. He is dead now and I guess it does not make any difference to the petroleum industry, but it made a difference to the 300 or 400 people who were laid off. That mine is still in operating condition and if we had a consortium we could pick up that mine.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to congratulate the new member for Eglinton (Mr. Parker). Earlier I was pleased to accede to the request of his leader and allow him to make his first speech in the House on the day of his first sitting. I wish him a long and successful career in federal politics and I am convinced that the entire country will derive benefit from his talents.
Having said that, I would like to comment on Bill C-7 even if in the past some members have accused the members of the Social Credit Party of Canada, to which 1 belong, of often

October 24, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
referring to money in their comments. Heaven knows we have been hearing about it for some time. Heaven knows that this small Bill C-7 which may appear insignificant-it has two pages at most-is deemed by the public as being of very minor importance.
However, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-7 includes a request by the government to the Parliament of Canada to increase its borrowing authority by the fairly large sum of $7 billion for the current fiscal year. This is a small bill but it has serious consequences. The estimates for the current fiscal year already provided for a deficit amounting to something like $11.5 billion; moreover, through Bill C-7, the government is asking parliament to give them an additional borrowing authority of $10 billion for the period beginning March 31, 1979 and ending April 1, 1980.
In both cases, it is stipulated in the bill that such loans will be used for public works and general purposes. However, Mr. Speaker, we are not told what are those general purposes. Is it to extend the Old Age Security Act to cover people who are between 60 and 65 years old? Is it to offer financial aid to the provinces so that in turn they can help municipalities where the property tax is too heavy for homeowners who can hardly finance the construction of roads, water works and sewers? Is it to increase funds for RRAP and the Canada Works program? There is no mention about it in the bill. But, in a question I put last week to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), I pointed out that the program was good but that it did not provide enough money for the provinces and the owners of homes in need of repair, so that in the end the program does not give the results we had hoped for. With regard to the Canada Works program whose budget was slashed by 20 per cent to 30 per cent, the situation is really deplorable at a time like this when unemployment stands at an extremely high level.
1 know of municipalities in my riding where the rate of unemployment is something like 58 per cent. Those are not my figures but those of people who were hired to make surveys and collect them; the manpower centres supply them to us.
Mr. Speaker, adding the figures in clauses 2 and 3 of the bill, we find that we are dealing with loans totalling $17 billion. That is why I said a moment ago that the bill is indeed very heavy, though it does not cover much paper. The interest on the increase in the national debt is roughly $18 million a day, which represents $6.5 billion for the current fiscal year. With these recent borrowings, we might have to pay even larger sums of money in interests, which will further increase the financial burden of the taxpayers.
Mr. Speaker, when an individual, a family or a corporation makes debts larger than he or it should, he or it goes straight to bankruptcy, and the same can be said of governments. How could it be otherwise? Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote some

figures so that the Canadian public, who have a right to know what is going on, can think about it and help parliament change what has to be changed if we are to improve the situation.
Has Canada's debt gone up or down in the last few years? Has the burden of our net national debt increased or decreased? We have to ask these questions and we have to get answers.
If so, would it not be urgent to change the way we finance the public sector? Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I believe it is the duty of this parliament to examine closely the alarming progression of the national debt. At the time the confederation was formed, on July 1, 1867, the national debt stood at about $75 million. Later on there was the cost of Canada's involvement in World War I as well as various other small undertakings that had occurred in the meantime, and also the economic crisis which lasted for ten years and was brought about by the crash at the New York stock exchange on October 24, 1929, exactly 49 years ago today, which is a sad anniversary but still an anniversary. The crisis was not triggered by Providence but by human beings, because the stock exchange is controlled by human beings, it is manipulated for one's own profit, it is operated by human beings, Mr. Speaker, and those who have a memory for facts must recall that during these ten years our country was poverty stricken, a great many Canadians experienced very serious difficulties, and this in an affluent society. I have known farmers in my area who did not have enough income to pay their debts, yet their stables were full of animals, their fields were producing bumper crops, but they were unable to pay, despite all the things they could sell, despite this plentifulness, there was nothing they could do, trade was paralysed, while in the cities, my God, people were dying of hunger because of a lack of distribution.
Afterwards, Mr. Speaker, our country's debt grew. Over 72 years our debt amounted to $3 billion, for 72 years, until 1939. By March 31, 1968, Canada's debt had reached $33 billion, and during that period there was World War II and other smaller conflicts like those in Viet Nam and in Korea where Canada participated, and we had to pay.
As of March 31, 1977, Mr. Speaker, nine years later, the national debt, as published in Hansard following a question I asked and which was answered on June 5, 1978, the net debt is estimated at about $67 billion and the way things go, I expect that by March 31, 1979 it will have soared to approximately $80 billion.
Mr. Speaker, we will not be able to continue to finance the public sector by this method without running the risk of leaving the next generation with a legacy of debts whose interest charge will paralyse economic progress and cause division between the various provincial and federal governments. That is not the way to ensure harmony in Canada. I have already said it in this House: it is the difficulties that governments have to find the money they need to meet their
October 24, 1978

obligations and carry out their responsibilities toward their people that divide Canadians; that is the heart of the problem.
Mr. Speaker, it is written in Bill C-7 that the borrowed Funds will be used for public works. I am in favour of that because public works are likely to boost the economy, provided they are financed the right way-that is not the way it is done now as we have to pay five times the value of the work done to get it done once. I happened to have in hand a letter from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation about a housing construction program in my constituency.
We, as members of parliament, are the ones who approve the funds needed by the CMHC to administer a housing program. And from time to time the CMHC enters into agreements with the Quebec Housing Corporation and as late as January 1977, the CMHC loaned $960,000 to the Quebec Housing Corporation for the construction of 40 housing units. But what is wrong with the system is that the Quebec Housing Corporation, through the provincial government, will have to tax Quebeckers at a rate of $4.93 for every dollar paid, which means that those people, who are Quebeckers, will have to pay for 200 housing units whereas only 40 units will be made available to the public.
Mr. Speaker, this is only an example of what is going on, and the same thing happens when the federal government builds, let us say, the Bank of Canada building across the street, the bank of all Canadians. Let us say the government will get the $50 million from chartered banks, either in bonds or otherwise, in order to put up that building, and will agree to reimburse $50 million over a 50-year period, and this at 10 per cent or 12 per cent interest rates. In other words, we would pay the cost of five of those buildings in order to get only one.
No doubt, Mr. Speaker, that I will be asked: What then is the solution you would suggest? The solution is this: to provide financing for the public sector, the federal government should use the services of the Bank of Canada. Some will say: But you will create inflation! You will put a lot of money into circulation regardless of the reality.
But, Mr. Speaker, what difference is there between putting $50 million into circulation after having borrowed it from financial institutions and putting that same amount into circulation after having borrowed it from the Bank of Canada? What difference does it make in terms of inflation? None whatsoever. But there would be a difference, for instance, in the public debt for, instead of paying 10 per cent or even 12 per cent interest the government would pay administration charges and that would not deprive the banks of their privilege to serve the private sector; on the contrary, they could better serve it and make the advance payments it needs to continue operating.
Mr. Speaker, that financing method must absolutely be changed, otherwise we are heading towards ruination. Public works! But they are necessary, and at the same time they would distribute money to the consumers; they will not buy out
Borrowing Authority Act
the Bank of Canada, but will have the money to buy consumer goods.
The Minister of Finance sitting on my right knows full well what I mean: He is the one who introduced a bill last spring inviting the provinces to cut their sales tax and give consumers more purchasing power. He did recognize at the time that Canadian consumers needed were purchasing power to buy more goods produced in Canada, to stimulate the economy of our country.
Mr. Speaker, there are also many things to be done all along the St. Lawrence, on both shores of the river. There are wharves going to ruin, others that must be preserved and others that cannot be maintained, depending on their future usefulness. When the municipalities come with their requests, the government says: We do not have any money for that. Retaining walls have also been built along the river. There are wharves like that in my riding everywhere. They are left to go to ruin. Private lands are in danger of being swamped over by the waves and when you ask the federal government to repair those works which cost Canadians a lot of money, there again they find all sorts of excuses to say that it is not the responsibilities of the federal government, go and see the provincial government. And when you do just that you are told to go and see the municipal government. Away you go to see the municipal government. They say: Well, we would like to but we do not have any money to finance that project. So everything goes to ruin because of a shortage of funds. Mr. Speaker, are we short of materials to provide those public services? Are we short of machinery? Are we short of workers to put the necessary materials together for those public utilities people could use? No. We have all that. What is missing? The dollar sign. The authorization to be able to carry out the work.
The Government of Canada just made a loan of $35 million to Cameroun for the extension of a wharf in the port of Douala. That is quite recent. That is a news published in today's Le Devoir. I have nothing against lending money to countries to improve their situation. The government made a 50-year interest-free loan with ten years of grace. About that, I once heard the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) answer a question put by my colleague and say: It is not interest-free, Canadians are paying the interest. That takes the cake, not only do we pay interest on our own borrowings but we have to pay interest on the handouts we make to foreign countries. That is nonsense! The government's classical answer is that those countries to which we are lending money will be buying Canadian products. Well, that is the least they can do.
I remember that during World War II I was a candidate in some by-elections and one general election. I heard such statements as: Canada lends money interest-free to England. Then, the ministers told us: Yes, but they buy our eggs, they buy our agricultural products. If a salesman were rich enough to advance enough money to his customers to empty his shop they would come and empty it, of course. But once the war was

October 24, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
over, when we stopped lending money to England, they stopped buying our products. I hope that the countries which take advantage of our generosity will not play the same trick on us so that one day we will be stuck with the debt without having the market.
Mr. Speaker, I have here a long list of the loans made to different countries which was issued on June 28, 1978. If you look up Hansard for June 28, on page 6830, you will see that with the exception of a single country, all these loans were granted interest free and provide for repayment in 50 years and seven or ten years of grace. For all practical purposes, this is nothing else but a gift.
You will say, Mr. Speaker, that we have to be human and understand that others have urgent needs. I agree, but I would like to emphasize the fact that money is considered as the true source of wealth and that it is given more rewards than the work of man. The construction worker employed on the site of the bank of Canada will be paid only once for having installed a tile and the necessary fittings and for having put some parts together. On the other hand, the capital borrowed to build this project will be rewarded five times. Dollar capital is rewarded five times and human capital or work capital is rewarded only once.
Mr. Speaker, this reminds me that one day not too long ago I had a discussion in a public service with a colleague who is familiar with financial matters and who argued that money is the true source of wealth. For my part, I argued that true wealth is in possessions. I gave him the following example: Two men go on a hunting expedition; one of them is an expert in financial matters, his wife loves him and believes that he is right; the other is a worker, perhaps a farmer or an industrial worker. The wife of the financial expert does not forget to go to the vault and to take two $100 bills to put in his wallet, while the wife of the worker takes two loaves of bread, a pound of butter and a few fruits and put them in a packsack. The two men leave for their hunting expedition in great humour. They do not have a very good sense of orientation. They do not have a compass. Night falls and they have to sleep in the forest. The next day is cloudy and foggy, and as they do not have the sun to guide them, they spend that day and the next one in the forest. I therefore asked my friend which one of the two was the wealthier? Was it the one who had two $100 bills in his pocket or the one who had bread and butter in his bag? He admitted that it was the one who had bread. I told him: "Sir, you are intelligent. Why is it that when you are in the woods, you can reason sensibly, and that as soon as you leave, you are unable to reason and lose all sense of proportion?
Mr. Speaker, in our country we have organized our society like this: the constitution provides for three levels of power, the legislative power which we represent in this House, the executive power which is the cabinet, the Minister of Finance, all his

colleagues and the Prime Minister, and the judiciary or the judges who examine our acts when taxpayers are not satisfied, who scrutinize our legislation and decide who is right and who is wrong. Above all this, Mr. Speaker, there is another level of power, about which the public knows generally nothing, least of all how it operates. It is the monetary power, the power to mint the credit of the nation, the power to influence the circulation of money and credit, the power to establish the duration of the circulation of financial credit, the power to require the repayment on terms fixed in advance failing which the product of your work will be seized. It is also the power to submit governments themselves by spelling out repayment and demanding as a guarantee the power that all governments have, that of taxing the citizens.
And, Mr. Speaker, this situation does not prevail only in Canada but every hon. member should have the time to read about this. I find it very interesting.
It was published in France, and I quote:
In France, money is where it is not needed and not where it is needed.
We could say that conditions are exactly the same in Canada. In the review dealing with monetary power, the following comment appears, and I quote:
The government and the banker of course are old pals. The government needs the banker who can provide his own credit. The banker needs the government because he must be under the cover of law and order.
Mr. Speaker, it is exactly like that in Canada. There is no difference. Things happen exactly like that and the article is entitled The real counterfeiters. Fet us speak of the loan that the government would like to obtain. Bonds will be issued. Some of them will be bought by our chartered banks and under the law, it is legal. The bankers who will purchase those bonds will merely create the necessary money. Why is the government unable to do such an operation through the Bank of Canada? We should have good accountants in that institution! This is why the government is- in a quandary and finds it difficult to do precisely what it wants to ensure the proper development of our society. Mr. Speaker, that situation is not news. In 1931, His Holiness Pope Pius XI denounced the power in the hands of private institutions. He said that this power is particularly noticeable among those who are the absolute masters and keepers of the money and mint the nation's credit as they see fit. He added that they control the economic blood of the nation to the extent that, without their permission, no one can even breathe. Nothing has changed since then because governments and parliaments, including ours, do not take the necessary steps to put some order in this field of activity.
Mr. Speaker, I want to catch the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). When we were considering Bill C-56, I promised him I would give him a copy of a bill which was studied by the American Congress and which gave the American government full power to control the money supply. I kept my word. I gave the bill to the President of Privy Council and
October 24, 1978

asked him to pass it on to the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance promised me he would consider it very seriously. I know he is a busy man, I know he is an overburdened man, but I still hope he will at least have enough time to take a look at it and that he will draw his inspiration from it when he will prepare his budget speech which he is supposed to table in the House in the near future.
Mr. Speaker, these are proposals which I consider serious and useful. I would just like to give the House an idea of what is the very substance of that bill of which I already gave a copy to the Minister of Finance. Here is what its introduction says:
To give Congress the constitutional power to issue money and control its value; to guarantee a minimum income to every American based on a stable and equitable assessment of the dollar whose value should always be high enough to allow the public to buy at will the goods and services that American industries and businesses can make available to them; put an end to the practice by which certain groups of individuals use and create bank deposits with fractional reserves.
This is exactly what is happening in Canada under the Bank Act, and specifically section 72. That is the basis of our system. I would like to reassure bankers, who may be watching us on television, that 1 am not personally attacking them. I respect them, they are human beings. They inevitably do great service to society, but it is the very system which the act of parliament grants them that I am attacking, because it gives bad results. We know what those results are, I just enumerated them: doubling our debt in nine years and increasing it from $33 billion to $67 billion. That is not a normal system. That a government be forced to go down on its hands and knees before financial institutions in order to obtain the funds necessary to administer the country, that is not normal. An individual or a company may be forced to accept such conditions because that is the private sector, it is the pressures of supply and demand, the pressure of competition. Mr. Speaker, I see that it is getting late, but I would like to quote the comments of a taxpayer published in the Wednesday, October 11, 1978, issue of the Journal de Montreal. Sometimes we think that people do not observe us, that they are indifferent to what leaders do, but here is what this man says in an article entitled "The world is heading toward disaster," and I quote:
Yes, you, our leaders, open your eyes, look around you and what do you see? Only depravation. The world is literally heading toward disaster. Animals and plants are disappearing, and you only think of wars and elections. For Heaven's sake, wake up! I think Canada, and indeed the whole world, should invest to save animals and trees. Look at the baby seals, the geese, the whales, make an assessment of the situation and you will see it is disastrous. Wake up and save the world! Be proud of being human beings, but show it. I hope that I have opened your eyes and that you are going to take the steps which are necessary.
It is signed by Christian Beauclair of Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, of course we have in our society leftists and rightists, and we have people who claim to belong to the centre right, and so on. But those who claim to belong to the centre right should examine their conscience.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-REDUCTION OF PERSONNEL-EFFECT ON SERVICE TO PUBLIC

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mir. Jean-Robert Gauthier (Ottawa-Vanier): Mr. Speaker, on February 7, 1978, the Leader of the Official Opposition in a speech to the Junior Chamber of Commerce in Toronto proudly announced a startling policy concerning the personnel of the Public Service of Canada. It will be remembered that Mr. Clark announced that a Progressive Conservative government would enforce an absolute freeze on the hiring of civil servants and that his objective would be to reduce the Public Service of Canada by at least 60,000 jobs in the next three years by not replacing employees leaving their jobs for the many reasons we know, namely retirement, death, departures, and so on.
That freeze coupled with a major cutback are certainly drastic measures, Mr. Speaker, designed to boost the popularity of the Progressive Conservative party by rejecting the odious nature of their economic measures on the public sector and more particularly civil servants. So in the few minutes I have I will be trying to show the danger of such a proposal and caution those who for partisan purposes would like to have Canadian taxpayers believe that if they were in power they would know how to show leadership and come down hard on the backs of federal civil servants by arbitrarily reducing their numbers.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot accept that concept of political machiavelism that the end justifies the means. They are not telling the whole truth when they are spreading this dangerous myth that by reducing the number of government employees through an absolute freeze and not replacing those who resign they will come up with savings big enough to finance a major reduction leading to substantial cuts in taxes. That is just not true.
Among the many questions which will need to be asked and which we are entitled to have answered, the leader of the Progressive Conservative party will have to say which government services will be cut. Does he have in mind the inspectors of the Department of Labour, or perhaps the scientists at the Department of Environment, or even worse, the professional analysts of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion? He will have to tell us which services will be discontinued or reduced. If he is suggesting he is thinking in terms of better manpower utilization, I would remind him that since 1975 there has been a significant decrease in the number of employees, and government managers are now working with a reduced staff that must meet the challenge and go on serving the Canadian people despite their reduced numbers. Moreover, it should be remembered that there is a competitive private sector, and if the workload of federal civil servants keeps growing without pay increases, they may prefer to find better jobs in the private sector. The impact would create problems at
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
the hiring end, with the danger eventually of depriving the public service of competent and hardworking personnel.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, if the Progressive Conservative leader came to power, does he want us to believe he can govern this country without government programs? Will such a potential government be a janitorial government leaving to the private sector the leadership in ideas and services in the eighties, or will they simply be the foreman of the status quo? That government will certainly wish to leave their mark and that of important ministers, put forward government programs, perhaps improve and even better explain, research, expand with the help of civil servants the whole range of existing services, and indeed create new ones.
It is intriguing at this point, at this time of serious disputes between labour and employers, to hear the opposition leader suggest he would replace the right to strike in the public service by a tribunal empowered to deal with disputes bearing on the public interest, his so-called Public Interest Disputes Tribunal which he would charge with solving disputes between labour and management. Is he proposing an agency without civil servants, one administered by computers?
When Mr. Clark talks about increasing employment counselling services to make it easier for the unemployed to find a job, is he trying to suggest that he will not hire qualified counselling personnel to provide this essential service? And finally, when he speaks about taking away the right to strike of federal public servants, is Mr. Clark suggesting that in his relations with federal employee unions, these workers will remain silent and not take part in the debate? This is obviously a proposal that can only incite to illegality, Mr. Speaker, because taking away the right to strike of federal public servants will not solve normal conflicts between employees and employer.
I understand, Mr. Speaker, that as serious and fraught with consequences as these issues may be, they can be considered hypothetical because, in my opinion, even if the Progressive Conservatives came to power they could not implement such a disastrous policy. An analysis of both proposals, that is the freeze and the non-replacement of public servants, shows the ambiguity and the cynicism of the Progressive Conservative leader since he did not explain to the Canadian people how he would implement such a policy. Mr. Clark speaks about the federal bureaucracy. We should know if this definition includes all government services and if it covers not only the employees under the jurisdiction of the Treasury Board, but also all others under federal jurisdiction, that is those employed by Crown corporations such as Air Canada which are responsible to the federal government.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I submit-and I asked the minister about this in the House last week-that it is impossible to administer Canada and provide Canadians with the services to which they are entitled under the laws passed by this House if there is a complete freeze of hiring in the public service and an
October 24, 1978

speakeroldname: Mr. Thomas H. Lefebvre (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-REDUCTION OF PERSONNEL-EFFECT ON SERVICE TO PUBLIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 must congratulate the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), who has shown once again his continuing concern for his electors, especially those who belong to the Public Service of Canada.
I cannot understand how anyone could pretend to serve the public interest by freezing hiring and simply letting the number of public servants go down haphazardly. The public service must implement the policy and the programs deemed necessary to provide for certain needs of the Canadian people. The number, the qualifications and the competence of the civil servants meet the criteria required to implement this policy and these programs. By allowing random cutbacks in the civil service, we would undoubtedly sacrifice essential tasks which are now being carried out. Since all such activities are linked to certain programs and certain services, these could no longer be maintained and the population would thereby be deprived of program or service which did meet their needs until then.
For instance must Canadian taxpayers accept cutbacks in medical services, in meat inspections, in food and drugs control or air traffic control? Should we let prison guards leave one by one or even all at the same time without ever thinking of replacing them? So the decisions related to the method and the speed with which to carry these cutbacks in programs and services would depend on the unpredictable decisions of civil servants to take their retirement or quit the public service.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this would be like putting the plough before the oxen. Those who leave the public service are not always those which it should be desirable to let go and those who stay are not necessarily the most indispensable elements. It is far better first to take the decision regarding the programs in a more rational matter and then readjust the size and the composition of the public service.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to follow up a question that I asked in the House yesterday. I put to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) the question whether the government has reconsidered its position with regard to Air Canada acquiring control of Nordair, or does the government intend to take the position that Air Canada should pursue that application? The minister replied in his usual studied and tortuous style, which consists not only of saying two hundred words when one of the words "yes" or
Adjournment Debate
"no" would satisfy, but which also conceals any hope for a reasonable answer.
In view of the answer given, which seemed to imply that the cabinet had not yet reached a decision on a matter which has been before it since June 29, 1978, I would like to ask the following question: Why has the government not taken a decision on this matter as yet? Even for this ridiculously inert and tardy government a decision should have been taken. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, I think this government acts as slowly as it thinks, which is below the speed limit in most provinces. It has often been said, Mr. Speaker, that silence is golden and patience is a virtue, but since the members opposite are hardly a gaggle of mutes, I suggest strongly that they finally act like a government and show some leadership. Since it is the government, it surely must face the inevitable task, no doubt unpleasant for them, of taking a decision.
In the proposed Air Canada takeover the facts are quite simple and a decision should have been reached by now. Air Canada proposes to buy Nordair for $25 million. The agreement in principle was the culmination of a number of conversations between the two companies in which Air Canada agreed to buy shares at $11.50 each. It is reported that Air Canada regarded the acquisition of Nordair as a sound business investment.
To argue that the deal would not be good for Air Canada would be senseless since Nordair is a very profitable company with a consistent record of profits and a sound financial position. However, while the acquisition of Nordair by Air Canada may be good for that Crown corporation, it is certainly not good for the Canadian consumer.
My party is against the acquisition of Nordair for many reasons. Firstly, this acquisition would harm air transport competition in Canada. As it stands today, Air Canada controls something like 60 per cent of air travel in Canada mainly due to restrictions placed on other airlines by the Canadian Transport Commission. Since 1970, for example, Canadian Pacific Airlines has been limited to 25 per cent of all transcontinental seats in this country. Its dominant market position and strong financial position of something like $20 million in profit last year enables Air Canada to ignore the consequences of competition. Last year, for example, the airline was able to ground itself for ten days at the mere rumour of a strike without even having to glance a nervous eye at the balance sheet. They knew that people in Saskatchewan-and I have a particular interest there-people in the maritimes-and people in the northern Ontario had no other alternative but Air Canada. Thus, neither strikes nor lockouts or whatever can drive passengers away from Air Canada, and the management knows it. The Conservative party does not intend to further strengthen this dominant position but to open the airways to more competition.
A second argument against the proposed acquisition is that it goes against stated government policy of preserving the essentially regional airlines to service local routes. Air Cana-

October 24, 1978
Adjournment Debate
da's takeover would introduce it to regional routes when its purpose should be national and international. Our party has stated that it would ensure that regional routes of less than 500 miles would be left to the regional carriers.
Thirdly, as the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs has noted, the proposed acquisition might violate provisions of the Combines Investigation Act and those of the National Transportation Act. Of course, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that this government will be overly impressed with this argument as its previous attitude toward the participation of other Crown corporations in unsavoury affairs, such as the uranium cartel situation and the sale of nuclear reactors, has already demonstrated.
A fourth reason for our opposition to the proposed acquisition lies in a suspicion of the motives of Air Canada. Air Canada has stated that its "acquisition of Nordair's highly successful charter organization would be of particular interest to Air Canada, because of the national airline's determination to become more active in the significant and growing area of operations and marketing". It must be remembered, however, that it was Air Canada that opposed the introduction of advance booking charters.
Finally, in times of supposed government spending restraints, and remembering the government's often repeated assertion, more often than not straight from the horse's mouth of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), that it wants to encourage the private sector, it does appear ridiculous to permit this government body to purchase a profitable public firm.
Our party has not been afraid to give leadership. I have outlined our position on the Nordair takeover this evening. In view of the continuing procrastination and monumental indecision on the other side as evidenced by the answers which I received the other day, I would strongly suggest to this House that it is not for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to come as he did into the House today and suggest that he is going to kick anyone in the slats, as he so eloquently put it, but for us to do exactly that to awaken this slumbering government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Thomas H. Lefebvre (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-PROPOSED STRIKE BY NORDAIR PILOTS-AIR CANADA CONTROL OF NORDAIR
speechtext:
In reply to the hon. member who raised this question, it might be valuable to put on record once again the main reasons why the Canadian Transport Commission did not turn down the application by Air Canada to buy out Nordair. They are as follows:
1.	Pacific Western Airlines acquisition of controlling interest in Transair gave western Canada strong regional carriers under common management and with common objectives. This created a need for strong regional carriers in eastern Canada operating from Montreal to Winnipeg. Nordair is profitable but the level of cash available has limited its dividends. The controlling shareholders wish to dispose of their interest in Nordair.
2.	Air Canada intends to operate Nordair as a separate entity and as a regional carrier under the regional air carrier

policy, the Aeronautics Act and the air carrier regulations. The act and the regulations would require the commission to approve any future merger of Air Canada and Nordair.
3.	It is not in the public interest that Nordair fail or not be able to replace equipment. Nordair's cash flow had not been acceptable to its shareholders and the only alternative acceptable to the shareholders is the sale of Nordair. If sale of Nordair to Air Canada is not approved, then the result would be a period of insecurity and instability with respect to Nordair operations.
4.	The acquisition of Nordair would not unduly restrict competition because there is little scheduled competition between regionals and there is limited competition between trunk carriers and regionals because of the regional air carrier policy. Financial results have not been satisfactory in spite of the limits on competition.
Points have been raised by nine petitioners, some of them very serious points. The government is giving close and careful consideration to all these matters. I can assure the hon. member there is no dragging of feet on this subject. The government is, as usual, taking a matter of such importance very seriously.

POST OFFICE-ALLEGED LOCK-OUT OF RETURNING STRIKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason I am rising tonight to take part in this adjournment debate is that Canada is in the midst of a postal strike which is causing serious disruption to our people. Delivery of family allowance cheques, social security cheques and accounts due to small businessmen and farmers is being withheld or delayed, and the over-all consequences for Canadians who are not involved in the strike in any way except as innocent third parties are tremendous.
The government used this situation as justification for asking parliament to legislate an end to this strike. Members of my party supported the government in this action. The post office provides an essential service; its activities are as important as those of any other single service throughout the economy and there is no way we can allow our people to continue to be victimized by these interruptions and stoppages. I urge the government to do its utmost to get the CUPW workers back on the job.
I hope the government will take full advantage of the provisions of the law which are available to ensure that members of the union who are on strike illegally return to work. If these measures fail, I believe that some of the 900,000 Canadians who are without jobs today should be given an opportunity to provide this essential service.
The reason 1 rise tonight to participate in this debate is that the government has spoken out of both sides of its mouth in this instance. In introducing legislation to legislate workers back to work last week, it indicated that the post office was an essential service and that Canadians could not afford to have
October 24, 1978

this essential service disrupted. That is a position with which I agreed, and the people at the post offices at Fergus and Orangeville in my area of Canada agreed with that very directly. Indeed, in the case of Orangeville during the last great postal disruption the workers stayed on the job, kept the post office open and provided service to some 12,000 homes which were served by the Orangeville post office and by the various subpost offices which are fed through the Orangeville post office. For their efforts they found themselves blacklisted by the union, and it was only recently that the local in Orangeville was restored to full union participation.
Leading up to this strike the members of the local at Orangeville took a look at the situation. They decided that in the national interest it was essential that this public service be kept in operation. They felt they had an obligation to the communities they served to stay on the job and to keep the mail flowing, and they voted in a very responsible way. They decided to stay on the job. In addition to that, they decided to write to some 94 different locals across the country to urge their workers to stay on the job. They signed the letter "from proud Canadians" and gave their names. In response to those 94 letters they received some 19 replies, of which only four were not favourable. It was clear from the responses that there was a strong sentiment in favour of keeping the post office open and working for Canadians.
Post office workers in Orangeville and Fergus reported for work on Monday and Tuesday of last week, and they kept service going for members of the communities served by those post offices. However, what was their reward for doing so? Their reward was to be told on Tuesday afternoon that they were not to report for work on Wednesday.
The Post Office Department denies that those workers were locked out, but there is only one word which applies when postal management, as a result of a labour dispute, decides not to allow people who want to work to report for work. Management locks them out. Management locked the doors of the post office and told its workers that they could not come in and that they could not keep the service going. Having crawled out on a limb to provide an essential service to Canadians, these dedicated and patriotic Canadians found that post office management decided to saw that limb off. I referred to that in the House of Commons last week as a disgraceful betrayal by post office management of those dedicated workers. If anything, those words are too generous to postal management, who decided to lock its workers out.
What were the results? The first was that, having jeopardized their relationship with their union, having run the risk of retaliation from people who were unhappy with the stand they took, and having decided to keep service going for the many thousands of homes in the communities they served, they found that the doors were locked by Post Office management, that they were refused work and that they were told to go home without pay.
Surely these workers deserve better. Surely Canadians deserve better. If there is one lesson to be learned from this, it is that if postal management and the government decide in the
Adjournment Debate
future that they want to ask dedicated public servants to put themselves on the line, to make sacrifices in the national interest and to set an example for the rest of Canadians-the type of behaviour necessary if we are to deal with our pressing economic and social problems-then it is incumbent upon the post office and the government to ensure that these people are not left alone out in the cold. These workers and Canadians as a whole deserve much better.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
subtopic: POST OFFICE-ALLEGED LOCK-OUT OF RETURNING STRIKERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to point out that on October 19 last the hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo (Mr. Beatty) misled the House. Knowing the hon. member, I am sure he would not do so intentionally. He said then and he said tonight that postal employees in Orangeville, Ontario were locked out and sent home without pay. Similar allegations were made by his colleagues, the hon. member from Oakville and the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall).

subtopic: POST OFFICE-ALLEGED LOCK-OUT OF RETURNING STRIKERS
speechtext: He will not be the hon. member for Oakville until after the election.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
subtopic: POST OFFICE-ALLEGED LOCK-OUT OF RETURNING STRIKERS
speechtext:
In misleading the House 1 think the hon. member is demonstrating a trait of Conservative members in recent weeks. They have been taking extreme licence with the facts and contributing to the climate of apprehension throughout the country regarding this urgent matter.
With some patience the minister explained in the House that there had been no lock-out as this term is understood in labour relations circles. Perhaps the hon. member for Welling-ton-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo does not fully understand the term "lock-out" as it pertains to management-labour relations. The minister said that employees were sent home for lack of work. Such action is known universally as a "lay-off', not a "lock-out".
I hasten to explain that lay-offs are general practice when there is no work for employees to perform. The post office has laid off employees when there have been legal strikes, but it is not the practice of the department to lay its employees off when some members are on an illegal strike. Before the passage of Bill C-8, the strike of CUPW workers was legal. After the passage of Bill C-8 it was no longer legal and employees who wished to work were encouraged to do so. Even though, I am sure, the distinction is quite clear to the hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo, he persisted in referring to what he called the disgraceful policy of lockout, and he reiterated that comment tonight.
Later, in response to a question from the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey), the minister further clarified the situation. Having consulted with his deputy minister and been assured that no cases of lock-out had occurred, the minister said:
There have been no "lock-outs" anywhere in the country, and therefore any employee who comes to work will be received and paid.

The minister went on to say that all post offices had been instructed to inform employees that they are welcome to come back to work and they would be paid. This statement has been repeated by the minister and by the department many times since. It has appeared in newspapers across the country and has had nationwide radio coverage.
Lest there be any doubt left in the minds of any members of the House, lest there be any doubt left in the minds of any
postal workers, let me state again: the post offices are open to receive their employees. Employees who wish to return will be welcomed and they will be paid.
